title: SLO-driven Interrupt Orchestration with Predictive KV Residency
creator: Asha Patel
description: Design and implement an interrupt orchestration layer for continuous batching that prioritizes tenant requests by SLO headroom while minimizing KV cache churn and GPU memory fragmentation. The goal is to maintain tail latency SLOs for high-tier tenants, reduce token-cost regressions from excessive KV eviction, and introduce a lightweight predictive residency model that anticipates hot KV entries to reduce unnecessary memory churn during preemption.
acceptance_criteria: Simulator shows <=2% increase in 95th percentile latency for P1 tenants under mixed workloads compared to baseline
KV cache eviction rate (items evicted per 10k tokens) reduced by >=25% for hot prefixes versus current greedy eviction under same load
No regressive increase in mean token cost for standard production RPCs (>0% increase will block release)
Feature gated rollout that can be disabled cluster-wide via config without node restart
Automated e2e job (bench/runtime) that validates interrupt decisions against golden prompt set
design_notes: We decouple 'interrupt orchestration' (who to interrupt) from 'memory reconciliation' (how to reclaim memory). This allows soft interrupts that avoid immediate KV eviction when alternative scheduling windows exist.
Introduce a compact predictive residency score per KV slab computed from recent access heat, tenant affinity, and token-length histograms. Score is updated with decay to avoid volatility.

Use a two-tier interrupt approach: (1) Soft-yield: pause in-progress batch execution at safe token boundaries and schedule continuation in next window; (2) Hard-preempt: forcefully reclaim GPU slab when headroom is exhausted and tenant is low-priority.
SLO headroom is expressed as a real-valued budget (ms) aggregated per tenant-class. Scheduler maps headroom to allowed interrupt frequency using an urgency curve (exponential at low headroom).
We prefer eviction lanes by residency score instead of LRU-only eviction. Hot-object preservation uses a conservative protected reservoir per GPU that is only trimmed under hard-preempt.
Trade-offs: predictive residency reduces churn but could misclassify ephemeral hot-shard bursts resulting in slightly elevated tail latency. We choose conservative thresholds during rollout.
Integration points: token-slicer, batch-allocator, kv-manager, tenant-metrics exporter. New gRPC control plane hook to adjust tenant urgency remotely for emergency throttles.
rollout_plan: Stage 0 (sim): run synthetic mixed workloads in simulator for 2 weeks and collect headroom and eviction metrics
Stage 1 (canary): enable soft-yield + residency scoring on 5% of runtime fleet during off-peak hours; monitor 95th/99th latency and KV churn
Stage 2 (gradual): expand to 30% if canary signals are green for 72h; enable hard-preempt thresholds only after 1 week of stability
Stage 3 (ga): feature flag on by default for runtime-1.22 with opt-out cluster config for risk-averse customers
Rollback path: toggling feature flag disables residency scoring and reverts to existing eviction policy; we retain telemetry to compare pre/post metrics
test_plan: Unit tests for residency scoring logic with synthetic access traces
Integration test that validates soft-yield resumes without KV eviction (end-to-end on dev cluster)
Load test that drives mixed-tenancy tail latency and verifies eviction and cost budgets under sustained pressure
Golden prompt regression: maintain a suite of customer-like prompts to ensure quality and token-cost stability
Chaos test: random node reboots while soft-yield is active to ensure no request corruption or KV state leak
metrics: Request requeue rate due to soft-yield (%)
implementation_notes: Scheduler will expose a per-request 'interrupt_hint' containing safe resume offsets to minimize recompute on resume
Residency score stored as a 16-bit fixed point with decay to keep memory footprint small across millions of entries
Hard-preempt triggers require two coordinated steps: (A) mark slab for eviction in kv-manager, (B) pause new batch allocations into slab until evacuation completes
We will reuse existing tracing spans and add a new 'interrupt.decision' span with decision reason and score to Speedboat traces
PRs: design doc at docs.internal/redwood/scheduling/interrupt-orchestration.md, initial simulator at github.com/redwood/sim/tree/interrupt-orch, runtime patch PR #1842
open_questions: How aggressive should decay be for residency score to handle diurnal tenants without penalizing bursty workloads?
Should protected reservoir size be a fixed percent of GPU memory or dynamic based on observed hit-rate?
What is the acceptable false-protect rate (hot objects mistakenly protected) before we shift thresholds?
Do we expose tenant urgency knobs to customers or keep them internal to Redwood ops?
